docs.title: split_lines()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def split_lines(content: str) -> list[str]:

Description: Splits source code into lines matching the line-numbering conventions of standard code editors and GitHub. It accounts for CRLF, CR, and LF line breaks while ensuring that a trailing empty string generated by a terminal newline is omitted.

Parameters: * content (str): Raw multi-line string content from a source file.

Returns: * list[str]: A list of discrete lines without newline characters.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

lines = split_lines(content)
return lines[:-1] if lines and lines[-1] == "" else lines
The helper normalizes raw line splitting by evaluating _LINE_BREAK_RE across the input string. Standard Python str.splitlines() splits on additional Unicode boundary codepoints (such as form feeds \f, next line \x85, and line separators U+2028), which diverge from GitHub's line counts. Slicing off an empty terminal item preserves strict 1-based alignment with standard text editor line numbers.

docs.title: class SourceIndex
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: class SourceIndex:

Description: High-performance normalized text-indexing structure created per source file. It pre-normalizes text to Unicode NFC, maintaining line-split, whitespace-collapsed, squashed, and word-token representations alongside character offset arrays to facilitate multi-tier substring searches.

docs.title: SourceIndex.__init__()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def __init__(self, content: str):

Description: Initializes the source index by pre-calculating normalized forms and inverted indices for fast quote location.

Parameters: * content (str): Raw string content of the target file.

Returns: * None

Raises: * None.

Example: 

index = SourceIndex(content)
During initialization, the class computes Unicode NFC normalized lines and creates four representations: line-delimited text (lines), whitespace-collapsed lines (collapsed) with cumulative character offsets (collapsed_offsets), fully whitespace-stripped text (squashed) with cumulative offsets (offsets), and lower-level regex word token lists (words). It also constructs an inverted index mapping each word to the line indices on which it occurs (word_lines), enabling rapid candidate filtering during token-based search fallbacks.

docs.title: SourceIndex.block_chain()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def block_chain(self, line: int) -> tuple:

Description: Lazily constructs and returns the enclosing block hierarchy for a specified 0-based line index, ordered from the innermost enclosing block to the outermost scope.

Parameters: * line (int): 0-based index of the target source line.

Returns: * tuple: A tuple of tuples, where each entry represents an enclosing block in the form (indent, text, kind, named).

Raises: * None.

Example: 

for indent, text, kind, named in index.block_chain(match[0]):
    if _names_in(text, parent):
        return True
This method provides lexical structural awareness without requiring full AST generation. It builds block chains across the entire document on first access via _block_chains(self.lines) and caches the result on self._chains. Each enclosing entry records the block's indentation column width, line text, structural category (e.g., container, function, control), and a boolean flag indicating whether the container explicitly defines a named scope.

docs.title: SourceIndex.text()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def text(self, first: int, last: int) -> str:

Description: Reconstructs the exact raw source code spanning a range of lines.

Parameters: * first (int): 0-based starting line index. * last (int): 0-based ending line index (inclusive).

Returns: * str: Joined original source lines separated by newline characters.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

index = SourceIndex(content)
raw_segment = index.text(m[0], m[1])
The method indexes directly into the internal self.lines slice [first : last + 1] and rejoins the elements using \n. It serves as the primary extraction mechanism when retrieving raw code blocks to evaluate child symbol definitions, determine error handling roles, or extract code excerpts.

docs.title: SourceIndex.locate()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def locate(self, quote, start: int = 0, end: int | None = None) -> list[tuple[int, int, str]]:

Description: Locates a claimed quote within a bounded range of lines using a 3-tier matching cascade: exact collapsed line matching, whitespace-squashed multi-line joined matching, and ordered identifier token sequence matching.

Parameters: * quote (Any): The substring or quote to locate in the source text. * start (int, default=0): 0-based start line boundary for the search. * end (int | None, default=None): 0-based end line boundary for the search.

Returns: * list[tuple[int, int, str]]: A list of matches formatted as (first_line, last_line, how), where how is "exact", "joined", or "tokens". Returns an empty list if unlocatable.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

matches = index.locate(evidence)
if not matches:
    rejected.append({"kind": "dependency", "target": target, "evidence": evidence, "reason": "evidence not in source"})
    continue
first, last, how = matches[0]
The location algorithm executes in three strict tiers. First, it searches collapsed_text using str.find and maps character offsets to line numbers using bisect_right; any match found on this tier is categorized as "exact". If no match occurs, it executes a "joined" search on squashed_text, permitting the quote to span up to _WINDOW lines (or the quote's own line count) while stripping all whitespace. If joined matching fails, it evaluates the quote's identifier tokens using _words_in_order anchored to the least frequent word via the inverted index word_lines.

docs.title: SourceIndex.excerpt()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def excerpt(self, first: int, last: int, quote) -> tuple[str, bool]:

Description: Extracts a trimmed, bounded source excerpt around the matched quote lines, capping the text size at _EXCERPT characters to prevent minified lines or large blocks from overwhelming the facts store.

Parameters: * first (int): 0-based starting line of the match. * last (int): 0-based ending line of the match. * quote (Any): The original quote to center within the excerpt if truncation occurs.

Returns: * tuple[str, bool]: A 2-tuple containing the extracted string excerpt and a boolean indicating whether the text was truncated.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

text, truncated = index.excerpt(first, last, evidence)
entry = {"target": target, "line": first + 1, **_end(first, last), "evidence": text, "match": how}
if truncated:
    entry["truncated"] = True
When the raw sliced text is shorter than _EXCERPT (300 characters), it is returned unmodified alongside False. For larger text bodies, the method collapses whitespace and centers a 300-character extraction window over the claimed quote substring. This ensures that essential identifiers and keywords remain intact within the stored facts artifact without retaining superfluous surrounding code.

docs.title: verify_file_claims()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def verify_file_claims(claims: dict, content: str) -> dict:

Description: Validates all raw LLM claims for a single source file against its text content. It coordinates symbol scoping, dependency location, configuration accessor ranking, and error role classification.

docs.title: Phase 1: Symbol Verification and Scoping
docs.text:
index = SourceIndex(content)
    result = {key: [] for key in CLAIM_KEYS}
    rejected = []
    claimed = 0
    unparsed = claims.get("unparsed", 0) if isinstance(claims, dict) and isinstance(claims.get("unparsed"), int) else 0
    if unparsed:
        claimed += unparsed
        rejected.extend({"kind": "unparsed", "reason": "reply item that is not valid YAML"} for _ in range(unparsed))

    symbols = _claim_list(claims, "symbols")
    claimed += len(symbols)
    kept, symbol_rejects = _verify_symbols(symbols, index)
    result["symbols"] = kept
    rejected += symbol_rejects
The function initializes a SourceIndex and accounts for malformed or unparsed LLM items directly as rejected records. It delegates symbol validation to _verify_symbols(), which scopes nested declarations to their parents and calculates line boundaries.

docs.title: Phase 2: Dependency Location
docs.text:
for item in _claim_list(claims, "dependencies"):
        claimed += 1
        target, evidence = _as_text(item.get("target")).strip(), _as_text(item.get("evidence"))
        matches = index.locate(evidence) if target else []
        if not matches:
            rejected.append({"kind": "dependency", "target": target, "evidence": evidence, "reason": "evidence not in source"})
            continue
        first, last, how = matches[0]
        text, truncated = index.excerpt(first, last, evidence)
        entry = {"target": target, "line": first + 1, **_end(first, last), "evidence": text, "match": how}
        result["dependencies"].append({**entry, "truncated": True} if truncated else entry)
Dependencies are checked to confirm that their quoted evidence exists in the file. Validated dependency claims record line numbers and excerpts; target-to-module resolution is deferred to verify_dependencies().

docs.title: Phase 3: Configuration and Error Classification
docs.text:
for key in ("config", "errors"):
        for item in _claim_list(claims, key):
            claimed += 1
            name, evidence = _as_text(item.get("name")).strip(), _as_text(item.get("evidence"))
            matches = []
            for first, last, how in index.locate(evidence) if name else []:
                if _names_in(index.text(first, last), name):
                    matches.append((first, last, how, False))
                    continue
                end = _call_span(index, first, last)
                if end > last and _names_in(index.text(first, end), name):
                    matches.append((first, end, how, True))
            if not matches:
                rejected.append({"kind": key, "name": name, "evidence": evidence, "reason": "name/evidence not in source"})
                continue
            roles = {m: _error_role(index, m[0], m[1], name) for m in matches} if key == "errors" else {}
            matches.sort(key=lambda m: (_ROLE_RANK.get(roles.get(m), 0), _name_rank(index.text(m[0], m[1]), name), m[3]))
            first, last, how, extended = matches[0]
            text, truncated = index.excerpt(first, last, evidence)
            if extended and not _names_in(text, name):
                text, truncated = index.excerpt(first, last, name)
            entry = {"name": name, "line": first + 1, **_end(first, last), "evidence": text, "match": how}
            if key == "config":
                entry["kind"] = _as_text(item.get("kind")).strip() or "config"
            else:
                entry["role"] = roles[matches[0]]
            result[key].append({**entry, "truncated": True} if truncated else entry)
Config and error facts expand matches across multi-line invocations using _call_span(). If multiple candidate locations match, matches are sorted by role priority (raised beats mentioned, which beats caught), naming prominence (code beats whole string, which beats prose), and span tightness.

docs.title: Phase 4: Deduplication and Normalization
docs.text:
for key, fields in (("symbols", ("parent", "name")), ("dependencies", ("target",)), ("config", ("name",)), ("errors", ("name",))):
        seen, unique = set(), []
        for entry in result[key]:
            marker = (*(entry.get(field) for field in fields), entry["line"])
            if marker not in seen:
                seen.add(marker)
                unique.append(entry)
        if key in ("config", "errors"):
            narrow_first = sorted(unique, key=lambda e: e.get("end_line", e["line"]) - e["line"])
            kept_spans = []
            for entry in narrow_first:
                low, high = entry["line"], entry.get("end_line", entry["line"])
                if not any(other["name"] == entry["name"] and low <= other["line"] <= high for other in kept_spans):
                    kept_spans.append(entry)
            unique = [entry for entry in unique if any(entry is other for other in kept_spans)]
        claimed -= len(result[key]) - len(unique)
        result[key] = unique
    result["rejected"] = rejected
    result["claimed"] = claimed
    result["found"] = claimed - len(rejected)
    return result
Duplicate extractions are deduplicated on identity fields and line positions. When configuration or error keys appear both as standalone calls and within larger enclosing expressions, the narrower source span is preferred.

Parameters: * claims (dict): Unverified dictionary of facts returned by an extraction LLM prompt. * content (str): Full text of the source file.

Returns: * dict: Verified claims dictionary conforming to VerifiedFileClaimsResult.

Raises: * None.

docs.title: code_view()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def code_view(lines: list[str]) -> list[str]:

Description: Produces a normalized view of source code lines where docstrings, block strings, and comments are blanked out while preserving exact line counts and character line positions.

Parameters: * lines (list[str]): List of source code lines.

Returns: * list[str]: Masked source code lines with comments and block strings converted to empty space.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

lines = split_lines(_nfc(content))
view = code_view(lines)
imports = {n for n, line in enumerate(view) if import_statement_like(line)}
The function scans line by line while tracking multi-line block string delimiters (""", ''', /*). When inside comments or multi-line strings, text is converted to whitespace or empty strings. Delimiters inside single-line strings (e.g., '"""') and asterisks forming glob patterns (e.g., lib/*.sh) are protected from accidental stripping. Lines starting with # or // remain in place so that subsequent preprocessor analyzers can inspect directives like #include.

docs.title: declaration_like()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def declaration_like(line: str) -> bool:

Description: Heuristically determines whether a source code line appears to declare a symbol (such as a function, class, constant, interface, or struct) across diverse programming languages.

Parameters: * line (str): Single stripped or unstripped source line.

Returns: * bool: True if the line matches structural declaration patterns, otherwise False.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

declarations = {n for n, line in enumerate(view) if n not in imports and enclosing[n] != "function" and declaration_like(line)}
This heuristic inspects modifier prefixes (_DECLARATION_MODIFIERS), declaration keywords (_DECLARATION_WORDS), uppercase constant assignments (_CONSTANT_RE), Haskell-style type signatures (_SIGNATURE_RE), SQL create statements (_SQL_CREATE_RE), and C/C++ style return-type signatures (_C_FUNCTION_RE). It ignores lines beginning with operators or closing brackets, distinguishing genuine symbol declarations from callbacks, expressions, and prose comments.

docs.title: import_statement_like()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def import_statement_like(line: str) -> bool:

Description: Identifies whether a source line represents an import or include statement across programming languages, filtering out assignments, expressions, comments, and inline calls.

Parameters: * line (str): Source code line to evaluate.

Returns: * bool: True if the line represents an import statement, otherwise False.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

imports = {n for n, line in enumerate(view) if import_statement_like(line)} | import_block_lines(view)
The function tests for leading import keywords (_IMPORT_WORDS), C-preprocessor includes (#include, #import), and dynamic loading invocations (require('...'), import('...')). It explicitly filters out assignments (e.g., source = 1), shell dots without file paths, and control structures (e.g., C# using (var r = ...)), confirming that the statement acts as a module dependency declaration.

docs.title: import_block_lines()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def import_block_lines(lines: list[str]) -> set[int]:

Description: Detects 0-based line indices located within multi-line Go-style grouped import blocks (import ( ... )).

Parameters: * lines (list[str]): List of source code lines.

Returns: * set[int]: Set of line numbers contained within grouped import blocks.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

found, inside = set(), False
for number, line in enumerate(lines):
    stripped = line.strip()
    if re.match(r"^import\s*\($", stripped):
        inside = True
    elif inside and stripped == ")":
        inside = False
    elif inside and _GO_BLOCK_LINE_RE.match(line):
        found.add(number)
The helper maintains a boolean state machine toggled on by import ( and closed by ). Inside this block, individual lines matching _GO_BLOCK_LINE_RE (bare or aliased quoted module paths) are flagged as imports even though they lack a leading language keyword on every line.

docs.title: enclosing_blocks()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def enclosing_blocks(lines: list[str]) -> list[str | None]:

Description: Determines the structural category of the enclosing block for each line in a source file by tracking indentation changes.

Parameters: * lines (list[str]): List of source code lines.

Returns: * list[str | None]: Parallel list where each element indicates the enclosing block category ("function", "container", or None).

Raises: * None.

Example: 

enclosing = enclosing_blocks(view)
declarations = {n for n, line in enumerate(view) if n not in imports and enclosing[n] != "function" and declaration_like(line)}
The algorithm maintains an indentation stack of (indent, kind) pairs. As indentation increases, newly opened blocks (function, container, control) are pushed onto the stack; as indentation decreases, closed blocks are popped. Control blocks (e.g., if, while, try) are transparently bypassed to associate lines with their true enclosing functional or container boundary.

docs.title: completeness_hints()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def completeness_hints(content: str, checked: dict, claims: dict | None = None) -> dict:

Description: Scans a source file for import and declaration lines that were not accounted for by any verified claim, highlighting missed symbols and dependencies for follow-up extraction queries.

Parameters: * content (str): Full text of the source file. * checked (dict): Dictionary of verified claims produced by verify_file_claims(). * claims (dict | None, default=None): Optional unverified claims dictionary.

Returns: * dict: Dictionary conforming to CompletenessHintsResult.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

hints = completeness_hints(content, verified_claims, raw_claims)
uncovered_lines = hints["uncovered"]
By cross-referencing lines flagged by declaration_like() and import_statement_like() against the line spans covered by verified symbols and dependencies, this function pinpoints gaps in LLM extraction. Declarations nested inside function bodies are excluded to avoid targeting local variables.

docs.title: unexplained_names()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def unexplained_names(content: str, source_path: str, depends_on: list[dict], table) -> list[dict]:

Description: Detects identifier tokens used within a file that are defined by exactly one other module in the project, but have no verified dependency linking the two modules.

Parameters: * content (str): Source code of the consuming module. * source_path (str): Path of the consuming module. * depends_on (list[dict]): Currently verified dependencies for the module. * table (ModuleTable): Global symbol and module routing table.

Returns: * list[dict]: List of dictionaries conforming to UnexplainedNameEntry.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

unexplained = unexplained_names(file_text, "src/api.py", verified_deps, module_table)
This diagnostic identifies implicit cross-module dependencies in languages supporting same-package or same-namespace scope sharing without explicit imports (e.g., Go, Java, C#, Elixir). It strips comments and strings (preserving string interpolations), computes local identifier bindings, and flags globally unique names from table.symbol_owner that appear in the code without a declared dependency.

docs.title: merge_claims()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def merge_claims(first: dict, second: dict) -> dict:

Description: Merges two claims dictionaries (typically an initial extraction pass and a targeted follow-up pass) while deduplicating entries based on their core identity fields.

Parameters: * first (dict): Primary claims dictionary. * second (dict): Supplementary claims dictionary.

Returns: * dict: Merged claims dictionary with deduplicated arrays and aggregated unparsed counters.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

merged = merge_claims(first_pass_claims, follow_up_claims)
The merge logic evaluates keys defined in _IDENTITY_FIELDS (e.g., (parent, name, signature) for symbols). If a claim in the secondary dictionary shares the normalized identity marker of an existing claim, the secondary entry is discarded to preserve the initial extraction metadata.

docs.title: normalize_name()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def normalize_name(text: str) -> str:

Description: Normalizes package, crate, and module names by converting them to Unicode NFC, trimming whitespace, folding case, and replacing hyphens with underscores.

Parameters: * text (str): Raw module or package name.

Returns: * str: Normalized, case-folded identifier string.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

clean = normalize_name("shop-core") # Returns "shop_core"
This normalization ensures that package references match across conventions. For example, a Cargo package defined as shop-core in Cargo.toml resolves correctly when referenced as shop_core in Rust use statements.

docs.title: verify_manifest_claims()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def verify_manifest_claims(claims: dict, content: str, manifest_path: str) -> dict:

Description: Validates extracted provides and aliases claims from package manifest files (e.g., package.json, Cargo.toml, go.mod) against the manifest's contents.

Parameters: * claims (dict): Claims dictionary containing provides and aliases lists. * content (str): Full text of the manifest file. * manifest_path (str): Repository-relative path to the manifest file.

Returns: * dict: Verified manifest dictionary conforming to VerifiedManifestClaimsResult.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

manifest_facts = verify_manifest_claims(claims, content, "packages/api/package.json")
The function verifies that declared package names and aliases appear verbatim in the manifest text. It uses _declares_name() to confirm that a claimed name acts as a declaration value (e.g., "name": "my-pkg") rather than a dependency reference (e.g., "dependencies": { "my-pkg": "1.0" }). Declared entry points and path mappings are similarly checked against the file text.

docs.title: manifest_rules()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def manifest_rules(manifests: dict) -> tuple[list, list]:

Description: Compiles verified manifest facts into package and path-alias resolution rules for ModuleTable.

Parameters: * manifests (dict): Mapping of manifest paths to their verified manifest facts.

Returns: * tuple[list, list]: A 2-tuple (packages, aliases) conforming to ManifestPackageRule and ManifestAliasRule.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

packages, aliases = manifest_rules(manifests_dict)
The compiler processes each verified manifest, resolving relative base directories and entry paths. Aliases are classified into "star", "prefix", or "exact" matching modes. The returned package rules are sorted with the longest name segments first, ensuring that specific sub-packages take precedence over root-level packages during import resolution.

docs.title: class ModuleTable
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: class ModuleTable:

Description: Project-wide resolution table for mapping imported target strings to concrete module file paths. It tracks repository files, single-owner symbols, directory hierarchies, and manifest rules.

docs.title: ModuleTable.__init__()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def __init__(self, paths: list[str], symbols_by_path: dict, contents: dict | None = None, manifests: dict | None = None):

Description: Constructs the resolution table by building path indexes, determining globally unique symbol owners, and registering manifest package boundaries.

Parameters: * paths (list[str]): List of all documented module file paths. * symbols_by_path (dict): Mapping of module paths to their verified symbol lists. * contents (dict | None, default=None): Mapping of file paths to raw text contents. * manifests (dict | None, default=None): Mapping of manifest paths to verified manifest claims.

Returns: * None

Raises: * None.

Example: 

table = ModuleTable(all_paths, symbols_map, file_contents, manifest_facts)
During initialization, the table indexes all file paths by directory and file extension. It extracts top-level symbols (excluding generic methods like get or to_h, which provide weak module ownership signals) and identifies single-owner symbols—names defined in exactly one module across the repository. It also runs manifest_rules() to register package scopes and path aliases.

docs.title: ModuleTable.normalize()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def normalize(self, target: str) -> tuple[list[str], str]:

Description: Deconstructs an import target specifier into path segments and an optional recognized file extension.

Parameters: * target (str): Raw import target string (e.g., "crate::store::Repo", "@/components/button", "./utils.js").

Returns: * tuple[list[str], str]: A 2-tuple (segments, extension) containing normalized path segments and the matched extension.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

parts, ext = table.normalize("utils.output") # (['utils', 'output'], '')
The method strips bounding quotes, brackets, and path prefixes (@/, ~/, $/). It extracts file extensions only if they match an extension found within the project's documented files. Segment separators (::, \, /, .) are normalized to slashes, and reserved path keywords (such as crate, super, self, and wildcard *) are discarded.

docs.title: ModuleTable.resolve_manifest()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def resolve_manifest(self, target: str, source_path: str, source_words: set, prefer_local: bool = False) -> tuple[list[str], str] | None:

Description: Resolves an import target using declared manifest packages and path aliases.

Parameters: * target (str): Raw import specifier. * source_path (str): Path of the importing source file. * source_words (set): Identifier tokens occurring in the importing source. * prefer_local (bool, default=False): When True, avoids matching manifest rules if a same-named local sibling file exists.

Returns: * tuple[list[str], str] | None: A 2-tuple (matched_paths, rule_prefix) if resolved, ([], "") if confirmed external, or None if no manifest rule matches.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

manifest_res = table.resolve_manifest("@lib/utils", "src/index.ts", tokens)
The method evaluates scoped path aliases from innermost manifest directory to outermost. If an alias matches (e.g., @lib/* pointing to src/lib/*), it resolves the target path directly. Otherwise, it matches target segments against registered package names. If a target begins with a multi-part prefix matching a declared package root, but the rest of the path cannot be found in the project, it returns ([], "") to mark the dependency as external.

docs.title: ModuleTable.resolve()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def resolve(self, target: str, source_path: str, source_words: set) -> tuple[list[str], str]:

Description: Resolves an import target to project module paths via relative paths, path suffix matching, directory packages, or single-owner symbol lookup.

Parameters: * target (str): Import target string. * source_path (str): Path of the importing source file. * source_words (set): Identifier tokens present in the source file.

Returns: * tuple[list[str], str]: A 2-tuple (paths, how) where how is "path", "package", "symbol", "ambiguous", or "external".

Raises: * None.

Example: 

targets, how = table.resolve("./client", "src/app.py", words)
Resolution checks relative paths first (./, ../, super::). For non-relative targets, it tests decreasing suffix slices of the target's segments against project module paths. If a unique module path suffix matches and satisfies _corroborated(), it returns (hits, "path"). If multiple modules match, it returns ([], "ambiguous"). If path matching yields no result, it checks whether the target points to a package directory or matches a globally unique symbol defined in self.symbol_owner.

docs.title: ModuleTable.used_names()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def used_names(self, path: str, source_path: str, source_words: set) -> set:

Description: Identifies owned symbol names of a target module that appear within the importing source file's identifier tokens.

Parameters: * path (str): Path of the candidate target module. * source_path (str): Path of the importing source file. * source_words (set): Set of identifier words present in the consuming file.

Returns: * set: Set of owned symbol names shared between the target module and consuming file.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

active_symbols = table.used_names("utils/output.py", "main.py", words)
This method filters the candidate module's top-level symbols against the importing file's vocabulary, excluding symbols that the importing file defines itself. For dotted names (e.g., Acme.Billing.Invoice), it tests for the terminal identifier segment as well.

docs.title: ModuleTable.namespace_members()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def namespace_members(self, target: str, source_path: str, source_words: set) -> list[str]:

Description: Identifies modules that belong to an imported namespace (e.g., C# using Acme.Accounting;) and contribute symbols used by the importing file.

Parameters: * target (str): Imported namespace string. * source_path (str): Path of the importing source file. * source_words (set): Set of identifier tokens in the consuming file.

Returns: * list[str]: Module paths declaring the namespace that export symbols used in the caller.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

members = table.namespace_members("Acme.Accounting", "Services/Order.cs", tokens)
The method trims trailing wildcards (such as .* or ::*) and splits the namespace into segments. It queries candidate modules that declare the namespace via declares_namespace() and checks whether the consuming source file uses any symbols owned by those modules.

docs.title: evidence_names_module()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def evidence_names_module(evidence: str, target_path: str, source_path: str, table: ModuleTable, how: str, relative_style: bool = False, per_line: bool = False) -> bool:

Description: Enforces the "evidence rule": a dependency claim is valid only if its quoted source line explicitly names the resolved module or an owned symbol.

Parameters: * evidence (str): Quoted source text provided as evidence for the dependency. * target_path (str): Resolved path of the target module. * source_path (str): Path of the referencing source file. * table (ModuleTable): Resolution table containing symbol ownership data. * how (str): Resolution mechanism ("path", "package", "symbol", "namespace"). * relative_style (bool, default=False): Flag indicating whether the language uses relative import paths. * per_line (bool, default=False): If True, evaluates multi-line quotes line by line.

Returns: * bool: True if the evidence explicitly names the target module or its unique symbols, otherwise False.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

valid = evidence_names_module(
    evidence="from utils.output import emit",
    target_path="utils/output.py",
    source_path="main.py",
    table=table,
    how="path"
)
The evidence rule verifies that the module's file stem appears as part of a path or import line, that the evidence contains a symbol uniquely owned by the target module, or that it references the target's directory on a wildcard import line. In languages that follow relative-import conventions (such as JS/TS), bare module names in quotes are prevented from resolving to local project files unless explicit relative syntax is used.

docs.title: declares_namespace()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def declares_namespace(content: str, dotted: str) -> bool:

Description: Checks whether a file's content contains a top-level namespace or package declaration matching a specified dotted identifier.

Parameters: * content (str): Source code of the module. * dotted (str): Dotted namespace string (e.g., "com.acme.billing").

Returns: * bool: True if a matching declaration line is found, otherwise False.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

has_ns = declares_namespace(content, "Acme.Billing")
The function splits the content into lines and checks for leading namespace keywords defined in _NAMESPACE_WORDS (such as namespace, package, or defmodule). If a line begins with one of these keywords and contains the target string, it confirms the file's namespace membership.

docs.title: scan_import_candidates()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def scan_import_candidates(content: str, source_path: str, table: ModuleTable, relative_style: bool = False) -> set[str]:

Description: Scans import lines in a source file to discover all project module stems referenced in import statements, serving as a recall diagnostic for missed dependencies.

Parameters: * content (str): Full text of the source file. * source_path (str): Path of the source file. * table (ModuleTable): Global resolution table. * relative_style (bool, default=False): Whether relative import conventions apply.

Returns: * set[str]: Set of module paths that appear to be imported.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

missed = sorted(scan_import_candidates(contents.get(path, ""), path, table, relative_style) - seen)
The scanner strips block strings and comments using code_view(), isolates import statements and Go import blocks, and checks whether any known module stem appears in a path context on those lines. Any candidate module identified by this scan that was not captured by verified claims is reported as "missed".

docs.title: relative_import_extensions()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def relative_import_extensions(located: dict) -> set:

Description: Detects file extensions that use relative import syntax (./ or ../) anywhere in the project.

Parameters: * located (dict): Mapping of module paths to their located dependency claims.

Returns: * set: Set of file extension strings (e.g., {".ts", ".js"}).

Raises: * None.

Example: 

relative_extensions = relative_import_extensions(located_claims)
This function inspects all located dependency targets across the codebase. If files with a given extension (such as .ts) use relative paths, that extension is flagged. In languages using relative imports, bare import specifiers (e.g., 'config') are treated as external packages rather than matching local files like config.ts.

docs.title: target_written()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def target_written(target: str, evidence: str) -> bool:

Description: Verifies that a claimed dependency target string is explicitly written within its quoted evidence line, rather than being an LLM paraphrase.

Parameters: * target (str): Claimed target module specifier. * evidence (str): Quoted line of evidence.

Returns: * bool: True if the target is found verbatim or matches a quoted path in the line, otherwise False.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

written = target_written(target, evidence)
For languages with quoted specifiers (such as JS/TS, Go, or C), the target must match a quoted string literal in the evidence, either entirely or as the tail of a dynamically concatenated path. For languages using unquoted identifier paths (such as Python, Java, or Rust), the target's identifier tokens must appear in order in the code, excluding any aliased bindings introduced by as or =>.

docs.title: judge_dependency()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def judge_dependency(claim: dict, source_path: str, source_words: set, table: ModuleTable, relative_style: bool, shadowed: frozenset = frozenset()) -> tuple[str, list]:

Description: Evaluates a single located dependency claim, determining whether it represents a verified internal dependency, an external import, or a rejected claim.

Parameters: * claim (dict): Located dependency claim dictionary. * source_path (str): Path of the importing file. * source_words (set): Identifier tokens in the importing file. * table (ModuleTable): Global resolution table. * relative_style (bool): Whether the module uses relative import rules. * shadowed (frozenset, default=frozenset()): External package names that shadow local modules.

Returns: * tuple[str, list]: A 2-tuple (verdict, details) where verdict is "depends_on", "external", or "rejected".

Raises: * None.

Example: 

verdict, detail = judge_dependency(claim, path, words, table, relative_style, shadowed)
The judgment pipeline first checks whether the target is shadowed by a known external import. It resolves the target against manifest rules via resolve_manifest(), then against module paths and symbols via resolve(). If a candidate module is identified, evidence_names_module() verifies that the evidence quotes the module or its owned symbols. If verified, it returns ("depends_on", [(module, how)]); otherwise, it returns a rejection reason.

docs.title: shadowed_names()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def shadowed_names(claims: list[dict], verdicts: list[tuple]) -> frozenset:

Description: Identifies bare package names that are targets of external imports and do not match any internal module import in the same file.

Parameters: * claims (list[dict]): List of dependency claim dictionaries for a file. * verdicts (list[tuple]): Parallel list of resolution verdicts from judge_dependency().

Returns: * frozenset: Set of bare identifier names that represent external dependencies.

Raises: * None.

Example: ``shadowed = shadowed_names(claims, verdicts) if shadowed: verdicts = [judge_dependency(claim, path, words, table, relative_style, shadowed) for claim in claims] 

If a file imports an external library such as `example.com/other/store`, the terminal segment `store` can collide with an internal project module named `store.go`. This helper identifies external package names so that subsequent symbol checks attribute references like `store.ErrNotFound` to the external library rather than misclassifying them as internal dependencies.

---

### `verify_dependencies()`
**Visibility**: Public
**Signature**: `def verify_dependencies(located: dict, contents: dict, table: ModuleTable) -> dict:`

**Description**: Resolves and verifies dependency claims across all modules in the repository, returning confirmed internal links, external dependencies, rejections, and missed import candidates.

**Parameters**:
* `located` (dict): Mapping of module paths to their located dependency claim dictionaries.
* `contents` (dict): Mapping of module paths to full text contents.
* `table` (ModuleTable): Resolution table initialized with all repository modules.

**Returns**:
* `dict`: Dictionary conforming to `DependencyVerificationResult`.

**Raises**:
* None.

**Example**:
```python
verified_deps = verify_dependencies(located_map, raw_contents, module_table)
The function processes each module, determining whether relative import conventions apply based onrelative_import_extensions(). It runsjudge_dependency()across claims, calculates shadowed names to avoid external library collisions, and re-evaluates claims when shadowing occurs. Confirmed links are recorded underdepends_on, while unreferenced import lines discovered viascan_import_candidates()are flagged undermissed`.

docs.title: facts_hash()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def facts_hash(signature: str, path: str, content: str) -> str:

Description: Computes a deterministic MD5 hex digest over an extraction signature string, file path, and file content to support caching of extraction facts.

Parameters: * signature (str): Extraction prompt version or tool signature. * path (str): Repository-relative file path. * content (str): Raw text content of the file.

Returns: * str: 32-character hexadecimal MD5 hash string.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

digest = facts_hash("extract_facts:v1", "utils/facts.py", file_text)
The digest binds the prompt schema signature, relative module path, and raw content together with pipe separators (|). Upstream pipeline caches use this hash to skip re-extracting unchanged files across repeated runs.

docs.title: source_commit()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def source_commit(local_dir) -> str | None:

Description: Retrieves the Git HEAD commit SHA from a local target repository directory via a subprocess call.

Parameters: * local_dir (Any): Filesystem path to the local git repository root.

Returns: * str | None: The 40-character Git commit hash, or None if the directory is not a valid Git repository or Git is unavailable.

Raises: * None (internal OSError and subprocess.SubprocessError are caught).

Example: 

commit = source_commit("/path/to/repo")
The function runs git -C <local_dir> rev-parse HEAD with a 10-second timeout. Standard output and errors are captured, and any operating system or subprocess failures return None to prevent Git inspection issues from crashing the pipeline.

docs.title: build_facts_document()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def build_facts_document(project_name: str, commit, modules: dict, manifests: dict | None = None) -> dict:

Description: Packages verified module facts, manifest rules, repository metadata, and schema version numbers into a standardized facts document dictionary.

Parameters: * project_name (str): Name of the codebase or project. * commit (Any): Source commit hash or identifier. * modules (dict): Dictionary mapping module paths to their verified facts. * manifests (dict | None, default=None): Optional mapping of manifest paths to manifest facts.

Returns: * dict: Document dictionary matching the FactsDocument schema.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

doc = build_facts_document("MyProject", "a1b2c3d", verified_modules, manifest_data)
The function constructs the root dictionary for facts.json. It stamps the payload with FACTS_SCHEMA, associates the commit hash and project identifier, and embeds a human-readable notice explaining that the document records verified facts rather than exhaustive symbol coverage.

docs.title: load_facts()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def load_facts(path: str, section: str = "modules") -> dict:

Description: Loads a specified section ("modules" or "manifests") from an existing facts.json file on disk, validating the schema version.

Parameters: * path (str): Filesystem path to facts.json. * section (str, default="modules"): Root key to extract ("modules" or "manifests").

Returns: * dict: Extracted section dictionary, or {} if the file is missing, invalid, or schema-mismatched.

Raises: * None (catches OSError and ValueError).

Example: 

previous_modules = load_facts("docs/api/facts.json", section="modules")
The function safely opens and parses the target JSON file. If the file cannot be accessed, contains invalid JSON, or declares a schema version differing from FACTS_SCHEMA, it returns an empty dictionary, allowing the pipeline to re-extract facts from scratch.

docs.title: save_facts()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def save_facts(path: str, document: dict) -> None:

Description: Atomically saves a facts document dictionary to disk as formatted JSON.

Parameters: * path (str): Target destination path for facts.json. * document (dict): Complete document dictionary to persist.

Returns: * None

Raises: * OSError: If directory creation or file writing fails.

Example: 

save_facts("output/facts.json", facts_doc)
To prevent file corruption during pipeline interruptions, the function first writes the JSON data (formatted with an indentation of 1 and UTF-8 encoding) to a temporary file ending in .tmp. Once writing succeeds, it calls os.replace to atomically swap the temporary file into the final destination path.

docs.title: facts_path()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def facts_path(output_dir: str, project_name: str, is_mkdocs: bool) -> str:

Description: Computes the target filesystem path for facts.json, placing it inside docs/api/ when MkDocs site generation is enabled, or directly in the project output root otherwise.

Parameters: * output_dir (str): Base output directory path. * project_name (str): Project identifier string. * is_mkdocs (bool): Flag indicating whether MkDocs documentation site mode is active.

Returns: * str: Normalized output path for facts.json.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

path = facts_path("dist", "core", is_mkdocs=True) # dist/core/docs/api/facts.json
When is_mkdocs is True, the file is positioned inside docs/api/ so that it is included in MkDocs documentation builds and preserved across CI cache runs. Otherwise, it is placed alongside the generated chapter markdown pages at the project root.

docs.title: Internal Constants and Regular Expressions
docs.text:
The module defines a series of internal limits, regex patterns, and keyword collections to support syntax analysis and line matching:

  • _WINDOW = 8: Maximum line span for joined multi-line quote matches.
  • _MIN_TOKEN_QUOTE = 3: Minimum number of identifier tokens required before falling back to ordered token matching.
  • _EXCERPT = 300: Maximum character length of stored source code excerpts.
  • _CALL_SPAN_LINES = 12: Maximum lookahead lines when expanding multi-line invocations like add_argument(.
  • _ROLE_RANK = {"raised": 0, "mentioned": 1, "caught": 2}: Priority ordering for sorting error matches.
  • _QUALIFIERS = set("./\\:\"'<")`: Punctuation characters that indicate path-like or qualified references.
  • _CLOSERS = set("\"'>")`: Trailing characters that close quoted path references.
  • _STRING_RE: Matches single-line string literals enclosed in single quotes, double quotes, or backticks.
  • _HANDLER_RE: Matches exception handling keywords (except, catch, rescue, recover).
  • _RAISE_RE: Matches exception raising keywords (raise, throw, panic, Errorf, etc.).
  • _COMMENT_START_RE: Matches the start of comment lines (#, //, /*, *, --).
  • _LABEL_RE: Matches goto labels, C++ access specifiers (public:), or bare keywords.
  • _NAME: Base regex fragment matching valid programming language identifier names.
  • _KEYWORD_BINDS_RE: Matches variable binding statements (for, let, var, val, const).
  • _LINE_BINDS_RE: Matches assignment statements (:=, =).
  • _KWARG_BINDS_RE: Matches keyword arguments within function calls.
  • _FIRST_NAME_RE: Matches standalone identifier names not preceded by a dot.
  • _DOTTED_RE: Matches chained identifier expressions (e.g., os.environ.get).
  • _SHELL_VAR_RE: Matches shell variable expressions ($VAR, ${VAR}).
  • _INTERPOLATION_RE: Matches string interpolation patterns (${...}, #{...}, \(...)).
  • _WORD_RE: Matches alphanumeric word tokens.
  • _LINE_BREAK_RE: Matches CR, LF, and CRLF line breaks.
  • _IMPORT_WORDS: Set of keywords that start import lines across programming languages.
  • _MODIFIERS: Common visibility and linkage modifiers (public, private, static, etc.).
  • _CONTAINER_KINDS: Identifiers representing compound types (class, struct, interface, etc.).
  • _OWNER_EXCLUDED_KINDS = {"method"}: Kinds excluded from assigning unique module ownership.
  • _NAMESPACE_WORDS: Keywords used in namespace and package declarations.
  • _INDEX_STEMS = ("mod", "index", "__init__", "init", "main", "lib"): Filename stems that serve as package index files.
  • _BARE_NAME_RE: Matches simple package names without directory separators.
  • _SEGMENT_RE: Matches individual path segments.
  • _GO_BLOCK_LINE_RE: Matches bare quoted paths within Go import blocks.
  • _DECLARATION_WORDS: Keywords that initiate symbol declarations across languages.
  • _FUNCTION_WORDS: Keywords that open function scopes.
  • _TOP_LEVEL_WORDS: Variable declaration keywords that declare symbols only when unindented.
  • _DECLARATION_MODIFIERS: Modifiers that can precede declaration statements.
  • _CONTROL_WORDS: Control flow keywords (if, for, while, etc.).
  • _CONTAINER_WORDS: Keywords that declare structural containers.
  • _BLOCK_CONTROL_WORDS: Keywords that open indented control blocks.
  • _CLOSURE_RE: Matches closure, lambda, and anonymous function heads.
  • _NAMELESS_DECLARATIONS = {"defstruct", "defexception"}: Container declarations that omit explicit names.
  • _TYPED_VALUE_RE: Matches statically typed variable declarations.
  • _WORD_AT_RE: Matches identifier tokens followed by whitespace or open parentheses.
  • _ANNOTATIONS_RE: Matches language annotations and decorators (@Override, @objc).
  • _PATH_TOKEN_RE: Matches path specifiers and quoted references.
  • _C_FUNCTION_RE: Matches C-style function definitions.
  • _CONSTANT_RE: Matches uppercase constant assignment expressions.
  • _SIGNATURE_RE: Matches Haskell-style type signatures (::).
  • _SQL_CREATE_RE: Matches SQL CREATE statements.
  • _EXPORTED_FUNCTION_RE: Matches CommonJS module.exports = function statements.
  • _NOT_IMPORT_AFTER: Punctuation characters following an import word that indicate an expression rather than an import.
  • _IMPORT_CALL_RE: Matches dynamic require/import invocations (require('...')).
  • _METHOD_RE: Matches method and function definition heads.
  • _CODE_TOKEN_RE: Matches multi-line block string delimiters and trailing comment markers.
  • _BLOCK_CLOSERS: Mapping of opening block delimiters to their closing tokens.
  • _IDENTITY_FIELDS: Mapping of claim categories to tuples of fields defining uniqueness.
  • _NAME_KEYS: Manifest keys representing declared package names.
  • _ENTRY_KEYS: Manifest keys representing entry point file paths.

docs.title: _nfc()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private Signature: def _nfc(text) -> str:

Description: Normalizes strings to Unicode Normalization Form C (NFC) to ensure consistent character representation across different operating systems and LLM outputs.

Parameters: * text (Any): Input object or string to normalize.

Returns: * str: Unicode NFC normalized string.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

clean_text = _nfc(content)
The helper wraps unicodedata.normalize("NFC", str(text)). LLMs occasionally output decomposed combining characters; normalizing to NFC ensures that characters match the precomposed forms standard in source code.

docs.title: _collapse()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private Signature: def _collapse(text: str) -> str:

Description: Normalizes a string to NFC and collapses internal whitespace runs into single space characters.

Parameters: * text (str): Input string.

Returns: * str: NFC normalized string with whitespace runs collapsed to single spaces.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

flat_signature = _collapse("def   run( self ):") # "def run( self ):"
The helper combines NFC normalization with Python's .split(), rejoining tokens with a single space. This produces a consistent representation for line-level quote matching across varying indentation styles.

docs.title: _squash()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private Signature: def _squash(text: str) -> str:

Description: Strips all whitespace characters from an NFC-normalized string to enable whitespace-insensitive matching across line wraps.

Parameters: * text (str): Input string.

Returns: * str: Contiguous string stripped of all whitespace.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

squashed = _squash("import { a,\n  b } from 'mod'") # "import{a,b}from'mod'"
The helper runs re.sub(r"\s+", "", _nfc(text)). This representation enables SourceIndex.locate() to match multi-line quotes across varying line wrap boundaries via simple substring searches against squashed_text.

docs.title: _words()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private Signature: def _words(text: str) -> list[str]:

Description: Extracts a list of alphanumeric word tokens from an NFC-normalized string.

Parameters: * text (str): Input string.

Returns: * list[str]: List of extracted word tokens.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

tokens = _words("class Cache_Manager:") # ["class", "Cache_Manager"]
The helper applies _WORD_RE.findall(_nfc(text)). These token lists feed token-fallback searches, symbol ownership checks, and token set comparisons in SourceIndex and ModuleTable.

docs.title: _has_words()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private Signature: def _has_words(text: str, name: str) -> bool:

Description: Checks whether the identifier word tokens of a target name occur in order within a body of text.

Parameters: * text (str): Surrounding source code text. * name (str): Name whose tokens must appear in the text.

Returns: * bool: True if all tokens of name appear sequentially in text, otherwise False.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

match = _has_words("def get_max_size():", "max_size") # True
The function extracts tokens using _words() and uses a two-pointer walk to check that every token in name appears in text in sequence. This permits punctuated names (such as CLI flags like --max-size) to match their underlying code identifiers (max, size).

docs.title: _names_in()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private Signature: def _names_in(text: str, name: str) -> bool:

Description: Checks whether a name appears within a text string, handling both standard word tokens and punctuated operator names (such as operator== or []).

Parameters: * text (str): Surrounding source text. * name (str): Name or operator symbol to locate.

Returns: * bool: True if the name or operator appears in the text, otherwise False.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

ok = _names_in("bool operator==(const Item& other)", "operator==")
For standard alphanumeric identifiers, this function delegates to _has_words(). For punctuation-heavy identifiers (such as C++ overloaded operators), it requires that both the whitespace-squashed name appears in the squashed text and any constituent word tokens appear in sequence, preventing operator matches from passing on partial token matches.

docs.title: _as_text()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private Signature: def _as_text(value) -> str:

Description: Coerces an arbitrary JSON or dictionary value into a clean string, converting booleans and None to empty strings.

Parameters: * value (Any): Input value of arbitrary type.

Returns: * str: String representation of the value.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

s = _as_text(item.get("parent"))
The helper handles loose typing in LLM output dictionaries, ensuring that booleans and None values evaluate to "" while numbers and strings are converted cleanly.

docs.title: _claim_list()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private Signature: def _claim_list(claims: dict, key: str) -> list[dict]:

Description: Safely extracts a list of dictionary claims under a given category key from an LLM claims payload.

Parameters: * claims (dict): Raw claims dictionary. * key (str): Category key to retrieve (e.g., "symbols").

Returns: * list[dict]: List of claim dictionaries, filtering out malformed non-dictionary elements.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

symbols = _claim_list(claims, "symbols")
The function verifies that claims[key] is a list and filters out any non-dictionary elements, protecting downstream loops from crashing on malformed LLM arrays.

docs.title: _verify_symbols()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private Signature: def _verify_symbols(symbols: list[dict], index: SourceIndex) -> tuple[list, list]:

Description: Resolves symbol declarations to their source lines, placing top-level symbols first and scoping nested members within their parent container's line boundaries.

Parameters: * symbols (list[dict]): List of extracted symbol claim dictionaries. * index (SourceIndex): Normalized index of the source file.

Returns: * tuple[list, list]: A 2-tuple (kept, rejected) containing verified symbol entries and rejection records.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

kept, symbol_rejects = _verify_symbols(symbols, index)
The verification algorithm executes in dependency order: top-level symbols are placed first, recording their line coordinates in placed. Member symbols are then resolved within the line span between their parent's declaration and the next top-level symbol. If a member's signature matches multiple locations, _parent_verdict() evaluates the enclosing block hierarchy to disambiguate the declaration.

docs.title: _end()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private Signature: def _end(first: int, last: int) -> dict:

Description: Constructs an {"end_line": n} dictionary entry if a match spans multiple lines.

Parameters: * first (int): 0-based starting line. * last (int): 0-based ending line.

Returns: * dict: Dictionary with 1-based end_line if last > first, otherwise {}.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

entry = {"line": first + 1, **_end(first, last)}
This helper injects 1-based end_line metadata into fact dictionaries only when an entity spans more than one line, keeping single-line records clean.

docs.title: _enclosing()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private Signature: def _enclosing(containers: list[tuple[int, str]], line: int) -> str | None:

Description: Identifies the nearest container symbol declared on a line prior to a specified target line.

Parameters: * containers (list[tuple[int, str]]): List of (line, name) pairs for known containers. * line (int): Target 0-based line index.

Returns: * str | None: Name of the nearest container declared above the target line, or None.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

parent = _enclosing(containers, match[0])
This fallback scopes symbols when structural indentation is ambiguous. It filters containers located above the target line and selects the closest predecessor.

docs.title: _parent_verdict()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private Signature: def _parent_verdict(index: SourceIndex, match: tuple, parent: str) -> bool | None:

Description: Inspects the text and enclosing block hierarchy of a symbol match to determine whether it belongs to a claimed parent container.

Parameters: * index (SourceIndex): Source index of the file. * match (tuple): Match tuple (first_line, last_line, how). * parent (str): Claimed parent container name.

Returns: * bool | None: True if the context confirms parentage, False if it contradicts parentage, or None if indeterminate.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

verdict = _parent_verdict(index, m, parent)
The check returns True if the match text explicitly references the parent (e.g., a Go receiver or C++ Class:: prefix) or if an enclosing block declares the parent. It returns False if an enclosing block names a different container or if the symbol sits inside a top-level function. If indentation cannot establish the relationship, it returns None.

docs.title: _in_parent()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private Signature: def _in_parent(index: SourceIndex, match: tuple, parent: str, containers: list) -> bool:

Description: Determines whether a file-wide match of a member symbol belongs to its claimed parent container, combining block verdicts with container position fallbacks.

Parameters: * index (SourceIndex): Source index of the file. * match (tuple): Match tuple (first_line, last_line, how). * parent (str): Claimed parent name. * containers (list): Known container declarations in the file.

Returns: * bool: True if the member belongs to the parent container, otherwise False.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

matches = [m for m in matches if _in_parent(index, m, parent, containers)]
This helper checks _parent_verdict(). If the structural block chain is indeterminate (None), it falls back to checking whether the closest container declared above the match via _enclosing() matches the claimed parent.

docs.title: _call_span()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private Signature: def _call_span(index: SourceIndex, first: int, last: int) -> int:

Description: Extends a match range forward across lines until unbalanced parentheses ( and brackets [ are closed, capturing multi-line method calls and argument lists.

Parameters: * index (SourceIndex): Source index of the file. * first (int): 0-based starting line of the match. * last (int): 0-based ending line of the match.

Returns: * int: 0-based line index where brackets balance, or at most _CALL_SPAN_LINES ahead.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

last = _call_span(index, first, last)
The function scans forward up to _CALL_SPAN_LINES (12 lines) past the match. It strips string literals via _STRING_RE and tracks the nesting depth of ( and [. Once the nesting depth reaches zero, it returns that line index, capturing multi-line signatures and calls without overrunning into function bodies.

docs.title: _name_rank()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private Signature: def _name_rank(text: str, name: str) -> int:

Description: Evaluates how prominently a configuration or error name appears within a source text match.

Parameters: * text (str): Source line text. * name (str): Target configuration or error name.

Returns: * int: Priority rank: 0 for code identifiers, 1 for exact string literals, or 2 for substrings within longer strings.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

rank = _name_rank("parser.add_argument('--port')", "--port") # 1
The ranking prioritizes code references (e.g., os.environ[KEY], rank 0) over exact string literals (e.g., "--port", rank 1), which take precedence over mentions embedded in documentation or prose strings (rank 2).

docs.title: _error_role()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private Signature: def _error_role(index: SourceIndex, first: int, last: int, name: str) -> str:

Description: Determines whether an error condition in a source match is raised, caught, or merely mentioned.

Parameters: * index (SourceIndex): Source index of the file. * first (int): 0-based start line of the match. * last (int): 0-based end line of the match. * name (str): Name of the error or exception class.

Returns: * str: Role classification: "raised", "caught", or "mentioned".

Raises: * None.

Example: 

role = _error_role(index, first, last, "ValueError")
The function analyzes the code preceding the error name on each line of the match (with string literals masked). It finds the positions of the last handling keyword (_HANDLER_RE) and the last raising keyword (_RAISE_RE). If a handler keyword appears after the raiser, the role is "caught"; if a raiser keyword appears last, it is "raised"; if neither keyword is found, it is classified as "mentioned".

docs.title: _find_closer()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private Signature: def _find_closer(line: str, closer: str, start: int) -> int:

Description: Finds the position of a multi-line block closer token (such as */ or """) in a line, ignoring occurrences of */ that form part of a glob pattern.

Parameters: * line (str): Source line text. * closer (str): Closing delimiter token to find. * start (int): Character column index to begin searching from.

Returns: * int: Character index of the closer, or -1 if not found.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

pos = _find_closer("/* comment */", "*/", 2)
The helper searches forward using line.find(). If the closer is */ and is immediately preceded by another slash (as in build/*/), it treats the token as a glob pattern rather than a comment closer and continues scanning.

docs.title: _rfind_closer()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private Signature: def _rfind_closer(line: str, closer: str) -> int:

Description: Searches backward from the end of a line for a block closer token, avoiding glob patterns.

Parameters: * line (str): Source line text. * closer (str): Closing delimiter token to find.

Returns: * int: Character index of the closer, or -1 if not found.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

pos = _rfind_closer(line, "*/")
The reverse counterpart of _find_closer(), this function uses line.rfind() to locate the last valid block closer on a line while ignoring glob sequences like /*/.

docs.title: _lead()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private Signature: def _lead(stripped: str) -> tuple[list[str], str | None, str, str]:

Description: Deconstructs the leading words of a source line, separating annotations, declaration modifiers, the first keyword, its following separator, and the remainder of the line.

Parameters: * stripped (str): Left-stripped source code line.

Returns: * tuple[list[str], str | None, str, str]: A 4-tuple (modifiers, word, separator, rest).

Raises: * None.

Example: 

modifiers, word, sep, rest = _lead("public static void main(String[] args)")
# (['public', 'static'], 'void', ' ', 'main(String[] args)')
The helper strips annotations via _ANNOTATIONS_RE and normalizes Swift-style access labels (e.g., private(set)). It iteratively collects keywords present in _DECLARATION_MODIFIERS, returning the list of modifiers alongside the first non-modifier token and trailing code.

docs.title: _indent()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private Signature: def _indent(line: str, tab: int = 4) -> int:

Description: Computes the leading column indentation width of a line with tab expansion.

Parameters: * line (str): Source code line. * tab (int, default=4): Spaces per tab character.

Returns: * int: Number of leading space columns.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

cols = _indent("\tdef run():", tab=8) # 8
The helper expands tab characters to space widths and calculates the difference in length after left-stripping whitespace, providing consistent indentation measurements across files with mixed tabs and spaces.

docs.title: _block_kind()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private Signature: def _block_kind(line: str) -> str | None:

Description: Classifies the structural block type opened by a source line ("function", "container", "control", or "other").

Parameters: * line (str): Source code line to evaluate.

Returns: * str | None: Block category string, or None if the line does not open a block.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

kind = _block_kind("class OrderProcessor:") # "container"
The function examines the line's lead tokens. Lines opening with function keywords or closure signatures are classified as "function"; class, struct, and module declarations become "container"; loop and conditional statements return "control"; and other indented constructs return "other".

docs.title: _nameless()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private Signature: def _nameless(text: str) -> bool:

Description: Determines whether a container declaration line defines an anonymous or nameless construct (such as companion object {, typedef struct {, or class << self).

Parameters: * text (str): Source line of the container declaration.

Returns: * bool: True if the container declaration introduces no named identifier, otherwise False.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

is_anon = _nameless("companion object {") # True
The function strips annotations and generic type parameters, then advances through container keywords and modifiers. If the remaining text lacks a trailing identifier name, it marks the container as anonymous, which alters parent resolution in _block_chains().

docs.title: _block_chains()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private Signature: def _block_chains(lines: list[str]) -> list[tuple]:

Description: Builds the enclosing block hierarchy for every line in a source file in a single pass using an indentation stack.

Parameters: * lines (list[str]): List of source code lines.

Returns: * list[tuple]: Parallel list where each element is a tuple of enclosing block records (indent, text, kind, named).

Raises: * None.

Example: 

chains = _block_chains(index.lines)
The algorithm iterates through code lines stripped of block strings via code_view(), maintaining an indentation stack with 8-column tab expansions. Empty lines, comment lines, closers, and labels do not alter the stack. For each line, the current active stack is recorded from innermost to outermost block.

docs.title: _name_segments()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private Signature: def _name_segments(text: str) -> list[str]:

Description: Normalizes a package or module name and splits it into discrete path segments.

Parameters: * text (str): Module path or package name.

Returns: * list[str]: List of non-empty segment strings.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

parts = _name_segments("@acme/billing-core") # ["acme", "billing_core"]
The helper normalizes the input using normalize_name() and splits on path and namespace separators (::, ., /, \, :), producing a standardized segment array for package matching.

docs.title: _declares_name()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private Signature: def _declares_name(line: str, name: str, keys: set | None = None) -> bool:

Description: Checks whether a manifest line defines a specified name as a declaration rather than as a dependency.

Parameters: * line (str): Manifest line text. * name (str): Claimed package name. * keys (set | None, default=None): Set of recognized declaration keys (defaults to _NAME_KEYS).

Returns: * bool: True if the line declares the name, otherwise False.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

is_decl = _declares_name('"name": "my-pkg",', "my-pkg") # True
The function splits the line at the target name and inspects the preceding tokens. If one of the recognized naming keys appears immediately before the name and is not enclosed within nested dependency blocks, it confirms the line as a genuine package declaration.

docs.title: _stem()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private Signature: def _stem(path: str) -> str:

Description: Extracts the filename stem (basename without file extension) from a path.

Parameters: * path (str): Filesystem or module path.

Returns: * str: Filename stem.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

stem = _stem("utils/facts.py") # "facts"
The helper combines os.path.basename() and os.path.splitext() to isolate the module name from its path and extension.

docs.title: _segments()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private Signature: def _segments(path: str) -> list[str]:

Description: Splits a filesystem path (excluding file extension) into individual directory and file segments.

Parameters: * path (str): Module path.

Returns: * list[str]: List of directory and filename components.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

segs = _segments("src/utils/facts.py") # ["src", "utils", "facts"]
The function drops the file extension and splits the remaining path on forward slashes, providing a segment list used by ModuleTable for suffix-based path matching.

docs.title: _is_relative()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private Signature: def _is_relative(target: str) -> bool:

Description: Checks whether an import target uses explicit relative path notation (./ or ../).

Parameters: * target (str): Import target string.

Returns: * bool: True if the target begins with a relative path prefix, otherwise False.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

rel = _is_relative("../common/config") # True
The helper normalizes backslashes to forward slashes and checks for leading ./ or ../, distinguishing relative file imports from bare package references.

docs.title: ModuleTable._suffix_hits()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private Signature: def _suffix_hits(self, tail: list[str], ext: str, source_path: str) -> list[str]:

Description: Finds project modules whose terminal path segments match a target suffix, preferring exact-case matches before falling back to case-insensitive comparisons.

Parameters: * tail (list[str]): Suffix segments to match against module paths. * ext (str): Optional file extension filter. * source_path (str): Path of the importing file (excluded from matches).

Returns: * list[str]: List of matching module paths.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

hits = table._suffix_hits(["utils", "facts"], ".py", "main.py")
The method matches tail against the trailing segments of all indexed module paths. If multiple modules match, it selects a candidate in the importing file's directory if one exists.

docs.title: ModuleTable._index_file()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private Signature: def _index_file(self, directory: str) -> str | None:

Description: Identifies the primary index or barrel file within a directory based on standard naming conventions (_INDEX_STEMS).

Parameters: * directory (str): Directory path to inspect.

Returns: * str | None: Path to the index file, or None if no standard index file exists.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

idx = table._index_file("utils") # "utils/__init__.py"
The method checks the directory's contents against _INDEX_STEMS in order of preference: mod, index, __init__, init, main, and lib.

docs.title: ModuleTable._resolve_relative()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private Signature: def _resolve_relative(self, target: str, source_path: str, source_words: set) -> tuple[list[str], str] | None:

Description: Resolves explicit relative imports (./, ../, super::) and leading-dot module paths against the importing file's directory.

Parameters: * target (str): Relative import target string. * source_path (str): Path of the referencing source file. * source_words (set): Identifier tokens in the source file.

Returns: * tuple[list[str], str] | None: A 2-tuple (paths, how) if resolved, or None if the target is not relative.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

resolved = table._resolve_relative("./output", "utils/facts.py", words)
The helper normalizes relative paths against the source directory using posixpath.join(). For Rust super:: paths, it traverses up the module tree, accounting for whether the source file acts as a directory index file.

docs.title: ModuleTable._resolve_rooted()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private Signature: def _resolve_rooted(self, base: str, source_path: str, source_words: set) -> tuple[list[str], str] | None:

Description: Resolves a normalized project-relative path to a specific module file or package directory.

Parameters: * base (str): Normalized project-relative path. * source_path (str): Path of the importing file. * source_words (set): Identifier tokens in the importing file.

Returns: * tuple[list[str], str] | None: A 2-tuple (paths, how) if resolved, or None.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

res = table._resolve_rooted("utils/output", "main.py", words)
The method checks for module files matching base with any recognized file extension. If no direct file matches, it checks whether base corresponds to a directory, returning the directory's index file and any contained modules whose symbols are referenced by the caller.

docs.title: ModuleTable._matches_whole()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private Signature: def _matches_whole(self, target: str, source_path: str) -> bool:

Description: Checks whether a documented file or directory path ends with every segment of an import target.

Parameters: * target (str): Import target string. * source_path (str): Path of the importing file.

Returns: * bool: True if an indexed module or directory ends with all target segments, otherwise False.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

matches = table._matches_whole("com.acme.billing.Invoice", "Main.java")
This check supports fully qualified package references (common in Java and Maven repositories). It confirms that the complete segment sequence matches an indexed module path without omitting leading segments.

docs.title: ModuleTable._resolve_in_package()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private Signature: def _resolve_in_package(self, package: dict, rest: list[str], source_path: str, source_words: set) -> list[str]:

Description: Resolves trailing import segments within a package boundary identified by a manifest rule.

Parameters: * package (dict): Manifest package rule dictionary. * rest (list[str]): Trailing path segments following the package name. * source_path (str): Path of the importing file. * source_words (set): Identifier tokens in the importing file.

Returns: * list[str]: Resolved module paths within the package.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

paths = table._resolve_in_package(pkg_rule, ["store"], "client.py", words)
If rest is empty, the method resolves to the package root. Otherwise, it searches for submodules within the package directory matching decreasing slices of rest, falling back to single-owner symbol lookup within the package if direct path matching fails.
